title: Be still (Psalm 46:10)
hookLine: be still, and know that I am God

lines: ON A MUG, BY A CALM LAKE.
cards: You've probably seen these words on a mug, a throw pillow, a calm lake photo, in soft script: be still, and know that I am God. It looks like a spa brochure. Here's the surprise.
The psalm that line comes from doesn't picture a quiet lake. It pictures the ground giving way, and a war. Mountains sliding into the sea.
Nations raging. Kingdoms toppling. Bows, spears and chariots.
And in the middle of all that noise, God speaks two words.

teach.h: A VERY PRESENT HELP IN TROUBLE.
teach.b: Psalm forty-six opens, in the King James Bible: "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble." Then it gets loud.
"Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed, and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea." The waters roar, the nations rage, kingdoms are moved, the earth melts.
Then the psalm turns: God "maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder."
Only then comes verse ten: "Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth." In Hebrew, be still is one word, harpu.

teach.h: HARPU — LET GO, DROP YOUR HANDS.
teach.b: Its root means to let go, to sink down, to let your hands drop, like soldiers told to lower their weapons, or someone unclenching after hours gripping the wheel. So it's less relax, more stop. Drop it.
Some scholars think it's spoken first to the warring nations: stop fighting, and know who's God. Others hear it spoken to the frightened people inside the city. Plenty of readers hear both.
This stillness isn't calm scenery. It's what happens when you stop trying to hold up the mountains yourself.

teach.h: BE STILL, AND KNOW THAT I AM GOD.
teach.b: Martin Luther loved this psalm; his great hymn A Mighty Fortress Is Our God grew out of it. Jews and Christians alike have prayed it in wartime, in plague and in grief. The pillow isn't wrong.
It's just missing the earthquake, and the stillness is meant for the moment everything is shaking.

how: Many Christians pray Psalm 46 in times of fear or crisis, and some use 'be still, and know that I am God' as a short prayer in silent or contemplative prayer, repeated slowly with the breath.

o: let go, drop your hands, stop the fight
relax and enjoy a calm, quiet moment
keep your body from moving as you pray

games.q: the earth shakes, the nations rage, the kingdoms totter. then God speaks. what does he say?
o: be still, and know that I am God.
games.why: "be still, and know that I am God." not relax, but let go: stop holding up the mountains yourself.

practice: Let your hands rest open in your lap, and notice where you're gripping, your jaw, your shoulders, your hands; let each one drop, the way the Hebrew word suggests.
Think of the thing that's shaking in your life right now, and don't solve it; just stop holding it up for a while.
If you pray, say the line slowly, once, be still, and know that I am God, and then stay still; if you don't pray, just stay.

wordCard.voice: Be still. In Hebrew, harpu: let go, drop your hands. Said in the middle of an earthquake and a war.

orig.note: Hebrew: let go, relax your grip, let your hands drop — rendered be still.

carryVoice: Your line: be still, and know. The mountains were never yours to hold up. That's day one hundred forty-five.
